headline: Did North Carolina's New Rule Double Its Mail-Ballot Rejections?
dek: A rule that took effect Sept. 4 spoils any mail ballot whose inner envelope isn't sealed. Rejections are up, but not double. Voters whose ballot was set aside get a new one, and can vote in person through 3 p.m. Oct. 31 or on Election Day, Nov. 3.
bottomLine: More North Carolina mail ballots are being set aside, but not twice as many as 2022 by the state's own count, and a voter whose ballot is set aside can still vote in person if there's time; those caught by Oct. 30 also get a new ballot by mail. The thing to do if you voted by mail: check BallotTrax, and seal both envelopes.

coreFacts.text: On Sept. 4, 2026, the day North Carolina began mailing absentee ballots, the State Board of Elections issued an updated Numbered Memo 2021-03 on a 3-2 party-line vote, its three Republican members for and its two Democrats against. Under it, if a ballot arrives with the inner "container-return" envelope unsealed, or outside that envelope, the county must spoil it (it is not counted) and mail the voter a new ballot package with a notice explaining the problem and the option to vote in person. Under the 2024 version of the memo, such a ballot was counted if the outer envelope was sealed.

body: On Sept. 4, the day North Carolina began mailing absentee ballots, the State Board of Elections changed how counties treat one common mistake. If a ballot arrives with its inner envelope unsealed, or loose outside it, the county now spoils it: the ballot isn't counted, and the voter is mailed a new ballot with a notice explaining what went wrong and that they can vote in person instead. Under the 2024 guidance, the same ballot was counted as long as the outer envelope was sealed. The board adopted the change 3-2 along party lines, its three Republicans for and its two Democrats against.

The change didn't come out of nowhere. After a lawsuit by the North Carolina Republican Party and the RNC, the board ruled on Feb. 2 that its 2024 guidance was "not correct," citing chain-of-custody concerns, and it adopted new rules in July. State law says a voter must seal the ballot in that inner envelope. But the July rules drew enough objections to be sent to the legislature, which won't take them up until after the election, so the Sept. 4 memo is what put the change in place.

A retirees' group, an Asian American group, a rural voters' group and two voters sued to block the rule. On Oct. 19, U.S. District Judge Thomas D. Schroeder said no. He wrote that changing the rules "is infeasible at this stage in the midst of voting," called the plaintiffs' 18-day wait to sue significant, and said a voter who fails to seal a ballot "has an opportunity to correct a mistake, and is not barred from participating in early voting or voting on election day." It was a preliminary ruling. The case goes on.

Then came the numbers fight. On Oct. 20, Gov. Josh Stein posted that the rules are causing "thousands more" rejections "at a rejection rate twice as high as in 2022." The State Board's spokesperson, Jason Tyson, said its preliminary data show a "slight increase": 3.1% this year against 2.6% at the same point in 2022. The News & Observer traced Stein's figures to a Democracy Docket report, which compared two advocacy groups' estimate of about 3% from 27 of the state's 100 counties with the nationwide rejection rate for all of 2022. The federal Election Assistance Commission puts North Carolina's final 2022 rate at about 2.2%.

The board's own daily file gives the statewide count. As of Oct. 21 it lists 156,092 mail ballots sent, 47,183 accepted, 1,936 received but not counted, and 106,973 not yet returned. Six days earlier, the not-counted column stood at 1,400. Mecklenburg (346) and Wake (315) have the most. The file doesn't say why each ballot was set aside: a missing ID or witness information also counts, not just a seal. Divided the simple way, 1,936 out of all returned ballots is about 3.9%, higher than the board's 3.1%. The board hasn't published its method.

A ballot set aside isn't automatically a lost vote, but the voter has to act. Mecklenburg County officials told The News & Observer they had rejected 257 ballots for sealing, about 4.6% of their mail ballots, and that 60 of those voters had since returned a new ballot or voted in person. Nobody publishes that figure statewide.

Mail is a small slice of this election. The board's Oct. 21 file lists 879,081 early in-person votes and 49,119 returned mail ballots, and mail requests were down 33% from 2022, WRAL reported. The risk grows near the end: if a sealing problem is found on or after Saturday, Oct. 31, there's no time to mail a new ballot. Staff must contact the voter that day and tell them they can still vote in person if there's time.

Both sides are spinning. RNC Chairman Joe Gruters said "Democrats and their allies tried to gut basic ballot safeguards in the middle of an election, and the RNC stopped them." The suit did come after voting began, and the RNC did help defend the rule, but the State Board also opposed the suit, the judge decided it, and the stricter rule itself took effect the day ballots went out. Stein's "twice as high" doesn't match the board's numbers. Common Cause's warning that "thousands" of ballots could be spoiled by Election Day is plausible, with about 107,000 mail ballots still out.

debate.argument: Voting by a noncitizen in a federal election is already a federal crime, and the Justice Department says every action it has taken is grounded in law and is being litigated in open court. A warning about the criminal code is not the same as intimidation, and the court has yet to say otherwise. Nevada's claim that all 185 names are citizens is the state's own statement, and DHS says Nevada already has the unique voter ID numbers it needs to check them. Mr. Blanche's line that state-facilitated fraud is unacceptable is unverified as a claim about any particular state, and I will not defend it beyond that.

body: On Oct. 20, the Democrats' Senate and House campaign arms, the Democratic Governors Association, Nevada's Democratic Party, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and a naturalized California voter sued President Trump, the Justice Department, Attorney General Todd Blanche, Homeland Security and DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin. The case, DSCC v. Trump, was assigned on Oct. 21 to Chief Judge James E. Boasberg in Washington, D.C.

They are asking the court to bar the administration from directing states to remove registered voters, withhold their ballots, or set aside or refuse to count ballots already cast. They also want the court to stop threats against state and local officials for issuing and counting registered voters' ballots. The suit claims the administration is acting beyond its legal authority and violating the Constitution's Elections Clause, the Tenth Amendment and the Voting Rights Act's ban on intimidating voters and the people who help them vote.

Nevada is the suit's lead example. DHS first announced it had found close to 16,000 noncitizens on the state's voter list. A DHS official later called that number "the ceiling" and said each voter still needed manual review. DHS then sent Nevada 185 voter ID numbers it said it was confident were noncitizens, said more than 14,000 others "need additional review," and declined to share the data it used to match them.

Nevada says its records show all 185 are citizens. "You have provided nothing of substance to suggest otherwise," a state lawyer wrote to DHS. Secretary of State Cisco Aguilar said the two sides may not even be looking at the same people, because DHS supplied only case numbers that can repeat across counties. DHS told PBS's Nevada Week that Nevada's claim it lacked enough information is "false" because DHS gave it "the unique state voter ID numbers assigned by the Nevada Secretary of State." "They have the data; they refuse to use it," DHS said. It did not answer when Nevada Week asked whether it still considers the 185 noncitizens, and said it had since manually confirmed about 2,000 more from the same list. RockLeak found no public list, method or court record behind that figure.

The suit also points to the threats. On Oct. 16, a Justice Department letter to Los Angeles County's lawyers said people who "knowingly tabulate ballots cast by individuals identified by federal agencies as noncitizens" risk "becoming aiders and abettors to a federal crime." That evening Trump posted: "They will all go to jail for a long period of time!!!"

That letter is part of a separate fight. DOJ sued California and Los Angeles County's registrar on Oct. 15 and on Oct. 19 asked a judge to make California set aside mail ballots from more than 20,000 people the federal government calls likely noncitizens until their citizenship is checked. On Oct. 21 that case was moved to Judge David O. Carter. As of that day's docket, no ruling had been made.

The administration says it is following the law. Federal law makes it a crime for a noncitizen to vote in a federal election. DOJ says DHS built its California list by matching the state's public voter roll against federal records, removing people with evidence of citizenship and manually reviewing the rest, and it said on Oct. 19 that it had charged 28 people on that list. Charges are accusations, not convictions. A DOJ spokesperson said its actions are grounded in law and being litigated in open court. Blanche said: "State-facilitated voter fraud is unacceptable in the United States of America." No court has found that any state did that.

The Democrats argue that the noncitizen voting law can be enforced only by prosecuting people, and that no law lets federal agencies tell states to hold back or set aside ballots. Neither judge had set a hearing or ruled as of Oct. 21, and Election Day is Nov. 3.

body: Russia released Stephen Hubbard on Wednesday, Oct. 21. Meeting U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff in St. Petersburg, Vladimir Putin told him Hubbard was already at the city's Pulkovo Airport. A video shared with CNN showed Hubbard meeting Witkoff there.

Hubbard is a 74-year-old retired teacher from Michigan. He was captured in eastern Ukraine in 2022. In October 2024, a Moscow court sentenced him to 6 years and 10 months for fighting as a mercenary for Ukraine; Russia's state news agency TASS says he confessed. His family and the U.S. State Department said the charges were fabricated, and the State Department designated him as wrongfully detained.

Trump announced the release on Truth Social. He wrote that Hubbard was freed "at the request of President Donald J. Trump, made directly to President Vladimir Putin in a telephone conversation last week," that the U.S. "was not required to give anything in return," and that "There was no 'swap' necessary for this release." Neither government has announced any prisoner going to Russia in return. Brittney Griner in 2022 and Evan Gershkovich and Paul Whelan in 2024 came home in prisoner swaps. Hubbard's is not the first recent release without one: CBS reports that Robert Gilman, a former Marine, was freed in August on a humanitarian pardon after a direct appeal by Trump to Putin.

Minutes later, Trump posted again: "Numerous people, who requested that sanctions be immediately imposed on Russia, have called to apologize to President Trump in that they didn't know that he was negotiating the release of Stephen Hubbard... If sanctions would have been placed, certainly those negotiations would have come to a complete and total halt." He named no one who apologized.

That post points back to Oct. 16. Five days before the release, Trump signed an order waiving tariffs and sanctions under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, a law the Senate had passed 86-11. Members of both parties criticized the waiver. Trump's two posts sit side by side: nothing was given, yet sanctions would have stopped the talks. Whether the waiver was part of the price, or a separate decision Trump links to the release, is not known from the public record.

The Kremlin's transcript of Wednesday's meeting adds one more detail. Witkoff opened by thanking Putin for freeing Hubbard and, later in the same remarks, after discussing the Ukraine talks, thanked him for Russia's decision to lift restrictions on diesel exports. Putin replied that Russia was preparing several tankers of diesel for the United States and that the first, of 40,000 tons, would leave in two to three days. That diesel deal was announced Oct. 9, after a Trump-Putin call, when Treasury also authorized certain Russian diesel transactions. The transcript does not connect it to Hubbard.

Witkoff called Putin "a humanitarian" and told him, "Because of you, he's going home to his family." Hubbard's son, Joseph Coleman, thanked Trump and U.S. officials and called the release "this humanitarian move by President Putin." ABC reports Hubbard's sister says he will be flown to San Antonio.

Hubbard isn't the last American held in Russia. CBS News reports that as many as 10 others, including dual nationals, are in Russian custody, and that he was the last one the State Department had formally declared wrongfully detained. CNN names several still held, including Andre Khachatoorian, David Barnes and Aleksander Antonov.

debate.argument: Both big prediction markets, where people put real money behind their views, price Hinson at roughly 58 to 59 percent. Iowa polls have missed the Republican number before: in 2020 the final average had Ernst up 0.4 points and she won by about 6.6, and in 2024 the last Selzer poll had Harris up 3 in a state Trump carried by more than 13. The current polling average has Hinson slightly ahead, and Fox's own Republican pollster points to the state's partisan makeup, with more voters identifying as Republicans than Democrats. Meanwhile NBC framed the first debate around Trump and mentioned Turek's missed votes only as Hinson's accusation, though PolitiFact had already rated a version of that attack True on Sept. 30. I can't show that markets are pricing in the polling misses, since no one knows why traders favor Hinson, and I won't pretend otherwise.
debate.concedes: Turek has real strengths. He leads among independents 51 to 31 in the Marist poll, Trump's approval in Iowa is underwater at 44 to 53, and he raised more than four times what Hinson did last quarter. Two of the five polls in 270toWin's average had him ahead, and so did a Fox poll with a Republican co-pollster, so calling this a toss-up is fair. Past misses don't guarantee a repeat, because pollsters adjust and errors can run either way. PolitiFact called Turek's claim that Hinson voted against ending the Iran war mostly accurate, which hurts her on his best issue.

consensus: All four analysts accept the record: the polls are close to a tie, both markets favor Hinson, Iowa polls underestimated Republicans in 2020 and 2024, and Turek outraised Hinson more than 4 to 1 last quarter while she kept more cash.
stillUnknown: Why traders favor Hinson. Markets don't explain themselves. Iowa's past polling misses and its Republican lean are plausible reasons, but no one can show that's what is moving prices.

body: Iowa's Senate seat is open because Republican Sen. Joni Ernst is retiring. The major-party nominees are Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson and Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek; Libertarian Thomas Laehn is also running. Election Day is Nov. 3.

The polls can't separate them. 270toWin's average of the five most recent polls, through Oct. 20, has Hinson at 46.4% and Turek at 45.6%. Three of those five have Hinson ahead: NPA Polling (Oct. 8–12) 47% to 44%, Trafalgar (Oct. 13–15) 46% to 44% and co/efficient (Oct. 15–19) 48% to 45%. Two have Turek ahead: Marist (Oct. 8–11) 48% to 45% among likely voters and YouGov (Oct. 6–12) 47% to 46%. Every lead is 3 points or less. Other averages differ on who is ahead: Wikipedia's compilation lists RealClearPolitics at Hinson +0.1 and Silver Bulletin at Turek +1.1 as of Oct. 19. The Cook Political Report has rated the race a toss-up since Aug. 20.

The betting markets are less torn. As of 10 PM ET on Oct. 20, Kalshi priced a Hinson win at 59 cents on the dollar and a Turek win at 44 cents; Polymarket had Hinson at 58% and Turek at 42%. Markets show what traders expect, not what will happen, and they don't explain themselves.

Why might traders lean Hinson? One possible reason: Iowa polls have missed Republican strength before. In 2020, the final 270toWin average had Ernst ahead by less than half a point; she won 51.8% to 45.2%. In 2024, the final Des Moines Register/Selzer Iowa Poll had Kamala Harris up 3, and Donald Trump won Iowa by more than 13. Fox News also reported that more Iowans identify as Republicans than as Democrats, and its Republican pollster, Daron Shaw, said "recent history and the state's partisan makeup suggest Hinson can pull this out." Most voters in Marist's poll agree with the traders: 59% of likely voters said they expect Hinson to win.

Why might traders be wrong? Marist found Turek ahead 51% to 31% among independents who are likely to vote, and Trump's approval among Iowa likely voters at 44%, with 53% disapproving. Pollsters change their methods after a miss, and a polling error can run in either direction.

Then there's the money. FEC reports filed Oct. 15 show Turek's campaign took in $13.9 million from July 1 to Sept. 30, more than four times the $3.25 million Hinson's campaign took in. But Turek also spent $12.6 million to Hinson's $3.1 million, so Hinson started October with $6.9 million in the bank to his $3.6 million.

The attacks have been fact-checked. PolitiFact, which rated a similar version True, confirmed Hinson's line that Turek was present for only 42% of Iowa House floor votes this year; he missed 261 of 445, which he says was because he was campaigning. It called Turek's charge that Hinson's husband was a "shadow lobbyist" misleading, and called his charge that she voted for the Iran war seven times mostly accurate: she voted against six War Powers resolutions to end it, and the seventh vote was about Lebanon. It found the law did not remove immigrants here illegally from Medicaid, since they were largely ineligible already, so reversing it would not put them "back on"; Hinson's campaign argued the law's provider-tax limits could lead some states to drop them from state-funded coverage. It also found Turek's "110,000 Iowans" health care figure counted more than that vote did.

What to watch: the campaigns' next FEC reports, covering Oct. 1–14, are due Oct. 22. They will show whether Turek's spending edge has kept up or whether Hinson's cash cushion is paying for a late push.

headline: DHS Swore About 189 Entries on Its California Voter List Had 'Minor Data Discrepancies'; LA County Calls List Unreliable
dek: Sworn filings in DOJ's suit to make California set aside mail ballots also describe 17,000 more records in review. In a 200-record sample, LA County found 42.9% were canceled registrations. California says its elections office never got the list. DOJ has charged 28 people on it.
bottomLine: DHS's sworn filings flag about 189 entries on its 20,000-name California list for data discrepancies and describe 17,000 more records in review. LA County's preliminary sample check found many canceled registrations and U.S. birthplaces, and California says its elections office never received the list. Twenty-eight people on the list have been charged. Whether the rest are noncitizens, and whether any ballots get set aside, is up to a judge who hasn't been assigned yet.

coreFacts.text: The Justice Department announced on Oct. 19, 2026, that it had charged 28 people in California with election-related crimes. All 28 are lawful permanent residents (green-card holders), 11 were arrested that day, and the department says all 28 appear on its list of "more than 20,000 likely noncitizen registrants" given to California officials. The release notes that charges are accusations and defendants are presumed innocent.

sources.label: DOJ press release 26-1222 (Oct. 19, 2026)
NPR

coreFacts.text: In the DOJ release's own descriptions of the 28 defendants, 22 are described as having voted, 1 as having submitted a provisional ballot and 5 as having registered without voting. Most face felony charges with a five-year maximum, such as false statements on naturalization papers or fraudulent registration. Six in the Eastern District face a misdemeanor charge of voting by an alien in a federal election, which carries a one-year maximum.

sources.label: DOJ press release 26-1222 (Oct. 19, 2026)
Newsmax (via Yahoo News)

coreFacts.text: In sworn declarations filed in federal court on Oct. 19, an HSI official (Eric McLoughlin) and a USCIS official (Nicolas Bartell) each said that USCIS "identified approximately 189 records with minor data discrepancies" on the list of over 20,000 individuals sent to California on Oct. 13, and alerted HSI. The declarations do not describe the discrepancies.

sources.label: Declaration of Eric McLoughlin, HSI (U.S. v. California, C.D. Cal. 2:26-cv-12025, Dkt. 22-3)
Declaration of Nicolas Bartell, USCIS (Dkt. 22-4)

coreFacts.text: Bartell swore that USCIS "has identified a separate batch of more than 17,000 voting records potentially tied to noncitizens after an initial review of voter rolls," and that "historically speaking, most voters in this initially flagged population will end up being referred to HSI." DOJ's court brief calls the 20,000 list "the floor" of potential noncitizen California voters.

sources.label: Declaration of Nicolas Bartell, USCIS (Dkt. 22-4)
DOJ memorandum supporting a temporary restraining order (Dkt. 22-2)

coreFacts.text: Bartell's declaration says USCIS "enhances" voter data "through a reliable third-party data analytics and investigative platform," pairs records with USCIS alien numbers, screens out people State Department and Social Security data identify as citizens or deceased, and then has investigators manually review the matches, with a second-level review. It says this process "is distinct from" the federal SAVE citizenship-check program.

sources.label: Declaration of Nicolas Bartell, USCIS (Dkt. 22-4)

coreFacts.text: According to DOJ's court brief, DHS Secretary Mullin wrote to California's secretary of state in July 2026 that a "preliminary review" showed there "may be as many as 190,832 noncitizens" registered to vote in California, including 81,336 registrants whose name, date of birth, address and Social Security number matched a noncitizen in DHS files. DHS told Newsweek the 190,000 remains its estimate and that the 20,000 are a manually verified subset.

sources.label: DOJ memorandum supporting a temporary restraining order (Dkt. 22-2), p. 23
Newsweek

coreFacts.text: California filed its opposition to DOJ's request for a temporary restraining order on Oct. 20. In a sworn declaration, state elections chief Jana Lean said California has more than 23 million active registered voters, that counties began mailing every active voter a ballot no later than Oct. 5, that no federal or state law requires officials to affirmatively verify a voter's citizenship, and that setting ballots aside "creates a substantial risk that a validly registered voter's cast ballot would be disqualified."

sources.label: Declaration of Jana M. Lean, California Secretary of State's Office (Dkt. 31-3)
Docket, U.S. v. California, 2:26-cv-12025 (CourtListener)

coreFacts.text: California's Oct. 20 court filing lists the judge as "Not Yet Assigned" and the hearing date as "Not Set." Los Angeles County Registrar Dean Logan also filed an opposition on Oct. 20, and two groups of civil rights and immigrant organizations have asked to join the case on California's side.

sources.label: California's request for judicial notice (Dkt. 31-4), caption
Docket, U.S. v. California, 2:26-cv-12025 (CourtListener)

coreFacts.text: In its Oct. 20 filings, LA County said 7,035 of the list's records have county addresses. In a preliminary check of 200, 42.9% were canceled registrations, 112 had not been mailed ballots because their records were canceled or inactive, and 71.2% had never voted. Among records with usable birthplace data, 38.9% listed a U.S. birthplace. The county's brief says the figures describe the records, not each person's citizenship.

coreFacts.text: A lawyer in the California secretary of state's office, Rachel Evans, swore on Oct. 20 that the office has not received the list referenced in DOJ's Oct. 13 letter, and that it has received federal grand jury subpoenas for voter records on about 300 people since August 2026.

debate.position: Washington is trying to protect the integrity of the ballot, and California's answer so far is to say that no law makes it check, which should worry every voter, not comfort them.
debate.argument: Twenty-eight green-card holders are now charged, and the DOJ's own descriptions say 22 voted and one cast a provisional ballot. All 28 appear on the list DOJ says it delivered on Oct. 13, and no ballots have been set aside. California's own elections chief swore that no law or policy requires officials to affirmatively verify a voter's citizenship at registration or voting; the check rests on each voter's sworn attestation. That is the problem. USCIS also swore to a layered process of data matching, then manual investigator review, then a second-level review. That is a serious process, not a guess. DHS's public wording about third-party software was muddled, though, and I will not defend that. The method details are still unverified, so the court should force disclosure fast, and the state should not simply decline to look.
debate.concedes: The strongest point for the other side is the risk to legitimate voters. The methodology is undisclosed, with no named platform, no match threshold and no error rate. USCIS itself found 189 records with data discrepancies, and California ballots are already in the mail. The 28 charged are a tiny share of 23 million voters and do not show how many of the 20,000 names are really noncitizens. Setting ballots aside could disqualify a validly registered voter, and a list with an unknown error rate is a weak basis for that.

California has 23 million active voters, ballots have been mailing since early October, and the state's elections chief swore that setting ballots aside risks disqualifying validly registered voters. DOJ also did describe a multi-step process with manual and second-level review, and California has not set any ballots aside. If the 20,000 holds up, that is a legitimate public concern.

debate.argument: Start with what the primary record shows. Weber's complaint about missing detail is fair, but it does not show the names are wrong.

They don't prove the 20,000-name list is clean. DHS told Newsweek commercial third-party data supplemented the records, and a USCIS official swore USCIS runs voter data through a third-party platform it doesn't name. DOJ calls its declarations 'more than enough', yet they don't name the platform, the match threshold or an error rate, and USCIS admits 189 records with data discrepancies. DHS still stands by its estimate of as many as 190,832, but its court list has 20,000 manually reviewed names, and a separate batch of 17,000+ is still in review. Citizens deserve a full account from both agencies and from Sacramento, which says no law requires its officials to verify citizenship beyond each voter's sworn attestation.

The state's elections chief swore that setting ballots aside risks disqualifying a validly registered voter's ballot. A list with unexplained discrepancies and no disclosed error rate is a weak basis for emergency action this close to Election Day. Also, the 28 charged are accusations, and the Nevada list shrank from up to 16,000 to 185 names.

consensus: All four analysts accepted every fact they debated: the 28 charges, the 189 flagged entries, the 17,000-record batch, the third-party platform and California's sworn warning about valid voters. LA County's sample check and the secretary of state's denial that it received the list were added to the record after the debate. All four agree the charges don't measure how accurate the list is and that the sworn filings disclose no error rate. They split on whether that should stop a court from acting or push California to check the names.

body: The federal government's list of more than 20,000 California voters it calls likely noncitizens has about 189 entries with "minor data discrepancies," according to sworn declarations filed Oct. 19. The same filings say a separate batch of more than 17,000 voting records has been flagged. RockLeak found no news coverage of either number.

The list is at the center of United States v. California, filed Oct. 15 in federal court in Los Angeles. The Justice Department wants a judge to order the state to set aside mail ballots returned by anyone on the list until their citizenship is confirmed. California filed its opposition on Oct. 20, and so did Los Angeles County's registrar. In a sworn declaration, Rachel Evans, a lawyer in the secretary of state's office, says the office has not received the list. An HSI official says he understands DOJ made it available to the office on Oct. 13. California's filing lists the judge as "Not Yet Assigned" and the hearing date as "Not Set."

Here is how the list was built, according to Nicolas Bartell of U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services. USCIS "enhances" voter data "through a reliable third-party data analytics and investigative platform" and matches it to immigration records. It then screens out people State Department and Social Security data identify as citizens or deceased, and investigators review the remaining matches by hand, followed by a second review. Bartell says this is separate from SAVE, the federal citizenship-check system. The filings don't name the platform or give a match threshold or an error rate.

A footnote in Bartell's declaration, and the same note in a declaration from Eric McLoughlin of Homeland Security Investigations, says USCIS "identified approximately 189 records with minor data discrepancies" on the list sent to California on Oct. 13, and alerted HSI. Neither says what the discrepancies are or whether those names were removed.

Los Angeles County, which received the list on Oct. 13, tested it against county records. Its Oct. 20 filings say 7,035 of the records carry county addresses. In a preliminary check of 200 of them, 42.9% were canceled registrations, 112 had not been mailed ballots because their records were canceled or inactive, and 71.2% had never voted. Among records with usable birthplace data, 38.9% listed a U.S. birthplace, which a county elections official called "strong evidence of citizenship." The county says the figures describe the records, not each person's citizenship. Its brief also cites the 189 discrepancies and the 17,000 batch.

DHS's public description is worded differently. Newsweek reported on Oct. 16 that DHS "disputed the characterization that USCIS used third-party software to conduct the analysis," while a DHS spokesperson said, in Newsweek's paraphrase, that commercial third-party data and other government data were used to supplement the public records. Bartell's Oct. 19 declaration says USCIS "enhances" the voter data through a third-party platform, then scores the matches and has investigators review them by hand. Neither names the platform.

The numbers have moved. In July, DHS Secretary Mullin wrote that there "may be as many as 190,832 noncitizens" registered in California, including 81,336 whose name, birth date, address and Social Security number matched DHS files. DHS told Newsweek the 190,000 is still its estimate and the 20,000 are a manually verified subset. DOJ's brief calls the 20,000 "the floor." Bartell swore that, historically, most people in a first-pass batch like the 17,000 end up referred to HSI.

On Oct. 19, DOJ charged 28 green-card holders in California and said all 28 are on the list. By DOJ's own descriptions, 22 voted, 1 cast a provisional ballot and 5 only registered. Most face felony charges, such as lying on naturalization papers. Six in the Eastern District face a misdemeanor charge of voting as a noncitizen. These are accusations, and the defendants are presumed innocent.

The two sides read this differently. Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter says California "refused to look at that list," and DOJ's brief says its declarations are "more than enough" to answer the state's doubts. The secretary of state's office swore it never received the list, and LA County, which did, checked a sample of it. California Attorney General Rob Bonta calls the 28 "a drop in the bucket" among more than 23 million voters. The state's elections chief, Jana Lean, swore that setting ballots aside "creates a substantial risk that a validly registered voter's cast ballot would be disqualified."

California also points to Nevada. There, federal officials cut an estimate of up to 16,000 noncitizens to 185 names, and the state wrote that "our records indicate that they were citizens." Nevada's secretary of state acknowledged that, because DHS sent only voter case numbers, the state may not have been checking the same people.

The group is Buckeye Freedom PAC. Its first two reports, filed Oct. 15, show $0 raised and $0 spent through Oct. 14. On Oct. 18 it reported two $600,000 payments for "media placement and production" to RFO Marketing Partners LLC of Wilmington, Delaware. The filing says the ads first went out Oct. 17.

The same day, it amended its FEC registration. It moved from Hudson, Wisconsin, to a PO box in Columbus, changed treasurers, switched to a bank in McLean, Virginia, and listed a contact email of electgop4usa@gmail.com. Its filings don't name a donor, and RockLeak hasn't seen its ads.

A second new group is working the other side of the race. Enough Promises Ohio registered Sept. 29. From Oct. 5 to Oct. 16 it reported $1.58 million: $1.06 million supporting Greg Levy, an independent socialist candidate, and $519,000 opposing Democrat Sherrod Brown. The AP reported that Enough Promises Ohio's mail vendor uses the same South Carolina office suite as a direct-mail firm run by Big Dog Strategies, which advises President Trump's MAGA Inc. super PAC and ran Republican Bernie Moreno's 2024 win over Brown. Politico reported that Husted's campaign said it had no involvement with the group.

Likely-voter polls with October dates range from Husted ahead by 2 to Brown ahead by 6. Whether any of this spending changes votes is unknown.

body: Texans started voting Monday, and the most expensive question in American politics now has a name attached: Elon Musk. FEC filings show Musk wrote two checks to the Senate Leadership Fund in September, $75 million on Sept. 9 and $83 million on Sept. 23. Each time, the Senate GOP's flagship super PAC moved the same amount the next day into Texas PAC, a new affiliate buying ads for Ken Paxton and against James Talarico.

All that money is chasing a race that, by most measures, is a coin flip. A University of Houston Hobby School poll of 2,000 likely voters, taken Oct. 10-14, has Talarico at 48% and Paxton at 46%, inside the ±2.19-point margin of error. Fox News' late-September poll showed a similar 51-49 split. No Democrat has won statewide in Texas since 1994.

Talarico isn't short of money either. His campaign committee reported $60.2 million in third-quarter receipts to the FEC, and the campaign says the total is $64 million counting its joint fundraising arm. He had $14.6 million on hand on Sept. 30, against $4.9 million for Paxton's committee. But outside spending dwarfs both campaigns: AdImpact data cited by the Texas Tribune shows outside groups had spent more than $217 million on ads by the end of September.

Paxton himself sounds uneasy about the help. In audio from a Sept. 24 lobbyist-hosted lunch in Washington, first published by Politico, the attorney general said, "I've never been in a race where I felt less control over the campaign." His campaign says he meant the legal wall between campaigns and super PACs.

The race has also been a test of how fast falsehoods spread. While Talarico was off the trail with the flu, conservative influencers on X spread a claim that he'd been treated at an Ohio mental health facility. The facility denied it, and the AP, Snopes and FactCheck.org all rated it false. Earlier, Paxton's campaign ran an AI-generated ad depicting Talarico reading from a fictional Bible, which FactCheck.org said stripped his real remarks of context and added words he never said.

Then there's the debate that isn't happening. Talarico has accepted several network invitations. As of mid-October, Paxton had accepted none, even after President Trump publicly called for a debate. That puts Texas on track for its first Senate race without a debate in about a quarter century.

Prediction markets lean Talarico. Kalshi traders put his odds at about 62% as of Oct. 20. But Tangle notes that polls underestimated Republicans in Texas in 2024 and 2022, and early voting runs only through Oct. 30. The $158 million question will be answered on Nov. 3.

headline: The Senate Voted 86-11 to Squeeze Putin. Trump Signed It, Then Waived Most of It.
dek: Two days before new Russia sanctions were set to bite, Trump set most aside with no end date. Older sanctions remain. Top Republicans are objecting.
bottomLine: On Oct. 16, Trump signed an order waiving most of the new tariffs and sanctions in the Graham Act, using a national-interest waiver the law itself provides. The waiver has no end date. Older U.S. sanctions on Russia stay in place. The move came a week after a deal to buy Russian diesel, and Republicans and Democrats alike have condemned it. Whether it helps peace talks or lowers fuel prices is unproven.

body: The Senate voted 86-11 to hit Vladimir Putin's economy with sweeping new tariffs and sanctions. On Sept. 18, President Trump signed it. On Friday, Oct. 16, two days before most of its provisions were set to take effect, he signed an executive order setting them aside.

The order invokes the law's own escape hatch, a Section 115 waiver allowed when the president certifies it is "in the national interests of the United States." It waives tariffs of up to 500% on Russian goods, up to 100% secondary tariffs on top buyers of Russian energy, and a long list of new sanctions. It sets no end date: the waivers last until the president or secretary of state decides otherwise. Sanctions imposed under earlier executive orders remain.

The timing points to diesel. On Oct. 9, Trump announced a deal with Putin to move Russian diesel onto world markets, and Treasury issued General License 135 the same day, authorizing Russian diesel transactions through April 2027. NBC reports diesel prices have climbed almost 70% since the Iran war began in February. CBS calculates the U.S. purchase at about 2.2 million barrels, just over half of a single day's U.S. diesel use.

Republicans didn't stay quiet. Sen. Thom Tillis called it "beyond irresponsible." Sen. Ted Cruz said, "I think it was a mistake." Sen. John Cornyn said Graham "would be appalled." Even Sen. Darline Graham, who was appointed to her late brother's seat and is now on the ballot, said she "would choose to keep the pressure on Russia." Democrats including Chuck Schumer and Richard Blumenthal went further, and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called the decision wrong.

The White House says enforcing the sanctions now would "impede ongoing U.S. efforts" to negotiate peace. Trump called it "a very good decision." Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the president wants 60 days to analyze the impact, although the order itself contains no such clock.

Can Congress stop it? Not before the election. Both chambers are in recess until after Nov. 3, and the waiver section requires only a certification and a report, not a vote. Rep. Gregory Meeks has introduced a bill to block the diesel deal, but it can't move until lawmakers return.

Traders aren't betting on a quick payoff for the peace argument. Polymarket puts a Russia-Ukraine ceasefire agreement by Dec. 31 at about 16.5%, and gives roughly 30% odds that Russian diesel actually lands in the U.S. by the end of November.

body: Twenty-two days before the midterms, federal agents showed up at a sitting congresswoman's home. On Oct. 12, Homeland Security Investigations agents searched Rep. Ilhan Omar's Washington home under a warrant the Justice Department says was judicially authorized, as part of "an ongoing federal criminal investigation." Eight days later, there are no charges, and DOJ hasn't publicly said what it suspects.

Reporting from several outlets, citing people familiar with the probe, points to immigration paperwork. Investigators are reportedly looking at whether Omar's late father lied or left information off his forms, and whether Omar was 17 or 18 when he became a citizen in 2000. Omar says she became a citizen before she turned 18. Grand jury subpoenas went to relatives, including, per The New York Times, her sister Sahra Noor. Agents took Omar's cellphone, and The Washington Post reported they took her passport too.

The search itself is now in dispute. In an Oct. 16 letter, Omar's lawyers say agents ignored a magistrate judge's instructions meant to protect her rights as a member of Congress: notify the House General Counsel and hand her the warrant at the start. DOJ says the letter is "riddled with false allegations and inaccuracies" and that it followed every court order.

Administration officials haven't been shy. Border czar Tom Homan told Fox News on Oct. 18 that denaturalization "could happen" "if the evidence points that way," and that he'd been told investigators have "a strong case," while saying he didn't know the specifics. DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin has repeated the claim that Omar married her brother, which Snopes rates unfounded and for which no public evidence exists.

Trump said the search had nothing to do with him and deferred to DOJ, but days earlier he told a Tennessee rally that "JD Vance and our people are looking at it very strongly." House Democratic leaders called the search "corrupt weaponization." NBC notes DOJ has no blanket 60-day pre-election blackout, but its policy says investigative steps shouldn't be timed to affect an election.

Some of this has come up before. A 2019 inquiry into Omar's immigration history found insufficient evidence for a full investigation, The Washington Post reported. A 2019 request by her staff to change her listed birth year with the Minnesota Legislative Reference Library is documented, but even Fox News notes it "does not establish that Omar falsified immigration records."
Traders are skeptical of a fast case. Polymarket puts federal charges by Oct. 31 at about 6.5% and by Dec. 31 at about 22.5%. Omar's Minneapolis seat isn't considered at risk on Nov. 3.
